description: The last ten centimeters of every press are not a muscle event, they are a tendon delivery, and the diamond push-up grades it honestly. Today you get your number, meet the triceps tendon that finishes every push you will ever make, and start building a lockout that does not fold.

scenes.narration: Get on the floor. | Hands under your chest. | Thumbs and fingers touching, | making a diamond shape. | Body in one line. | Now lower yourself down | until your chest | touches your hands, | and press back up | to a full lockout. | Elbows completely straight. | That is one rep. | Count your clean reps | until the lockout fails. | No sagging hips. | No bent-arm finishes. | When the last centimeters | stop happening honestly, | the test is over. | That number is yours. | Write it down. | Before this video ends | I will tell you | what it really means. | The top of the rep | is where tendons talk.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN FOLDING AND FINISHING
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Fifteen clean diamond push-ups is where a folding lockout becomes a finishing one. Under eight, your triceps tendon has been quitting early and your chest has been covering for it, which is why your pressing stalls at the top. Over twenty-five, you own a lockout most bigger men cannot match, because the end of the rep is the part nobody trains. Notice where this test is won and lost. Not at the bottom, where the chest is strong. At the very top, in the last ten centimeters, where a single tendon has to deliver everything.
scenes.sub: under 8: lockout quits early - over 25: pressing power

lines: into one tendon at the elbow.
beats.title: THE DELIVERY POINT

scenes.narration: Look at the back of your arm. The triceps is three muscles, three heads, and they look impressive in a mirror. But all three heads merge, just above your elbow, into a single tendon that grips the point of the elbow bone. Every gram of force those three heads produce has to pass through that one delivery point. If the tendon is soft and undertrained, the delivery leaks. The muscle contracts, the cable stretches, and the last part of the press arrives late and weak. This is the hidden reason some guys are strong off the chest and helpless at the top. Their engines are fine. Their gate is narrow. The diamond push-up is the purest test of that gate because the narrow hand position removes the chest from the story and loads the triceps tendon almost alone. When your lockout folds at rep nine, it is not your chest giving up. It is a single tendon at the back of your elbow, reporting that it has never been trained to deliver under fatigue. Gates can be widened. That is what the rest of this video is for.

beats.text: THE HARDEST PART IS THE SHORTEST

scenes.narration: Now the physics that makes this test so honest. In a push-up, the bottom feels hard because your chest is stretched. But the demand on the triceps tendon climbs as you press, and it peaks near the top, where the elbow straightens and the tendon has to deliver maximum force through the smallest margin for error. This is called the strength curve, and it lies to lifters. They judge their pressing by how the heavy bottom feels, then wonder why they fail at the top where it felt easy in warm-ups. The answer is that the top is a different exercise, run by a different tissue. Training only full reps trains it for a second per rep. Training the lockout itself, with pauses and slow finishes, gives the tendon the long, heavy seconds it actually adapts to. There is a simple way to feel this yourself. Do one diamond push-up as slowly as you can, and notice where the shaking starts. It will not be at the bottom. It will be in the final stretch, elbows almost straight, where the triceps tendon is working alone with no chest left to hide behind. That shake is the sound of the gate being measured. Your diamond number is low exactly where the tendon is undertrained, and it will climb fastest exactly there too.

There is a bigger cousin of this test worth knowing about: the dip. Between two chairs, your triceps tendon takes most of your bodyweight through a deep elbow bend, which is why dips build legendary lockout strength and why they humble beginners so fast. But notice the order of operations. The dip loads the tendon heavily through a long range, and a tendon that has never been graded on the floor is not ready for it. The diamond push-up is the dip's honest little brother. It tells you, with no equipment and no danger, exactly how much delivery your elbow gate can handle today. Master the floor version, earn your fifteen, and the dip becomes a progression instead of a punishment. This channel always grades before it loads. The number first, the ego second.

lines: more reps to train the gate.
beats.title: YOUR WEIGHT IS THE LOAD

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage in the diamond. A punch, a press and a push-up all end at the same place: a straight elbow delivering force. The lighter you are, the more clean reps you can stack before fatigue ruins your form, and reps are the currency this tendon accepts. Heavy guys often fail diamonds early because every rep costs them more, so they practice the lockout less, so it stays their weakest link forever. You get the opposite spiral. More reps, more practice, a wider gate, and a lockout that becomes the strongest part of your press while bigger men are still folding at the top.

Now we train the gate together. Diamonds, clean reps, full lockout every time. Forty seconds of work, twenty to rest, three rounds. When the lockout stops being honest, the set is done, no matter what the clock says. Press. Go.

Here is your week. The three rounds you just did, three days a week, with one upgrade: pause for a full second at every lockout. That pause is not decoration. It is the exact second the tendon is under peak load, and stacking it rep after rep is how the gate widens. Now the mistakes. Mistake one: bent-arm finishes. A rep that ends with soft elbows is a rep the tendon never got. Straighten fully or do not count it. Mistake two: sagging hips to steal reps. That changes the angle and hands the work back to the chest. Mistake three: flaring the elbows wide to escape. Keep them tracking close to your ribs, where the triceps tendon owns the movement. One extra clean rep a week sounds slow. In six months it is twenty-six reps of delivery you did not have, through a gate most men never widen.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME DIAMOND, SAME RULES
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under eight: the gate is narrow, and your press has been leaking at the top for as long as you have trained. Eight to fifteen: the delivery is engaging, lockouts are getting honest. Over fifteen: a finishing press, the kind that does not fold under fatigue. Over twenty-five: pressing power territory, and your elbows deliver more than men twice your size. Put your number in the comments. Just the reps. In thirty days we make the diamond again and re-grade the gate.
scenes.sub: comment your number below - then beat it

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now the diamond comes back, and the last ten centimeters will tell the truth about your training. Subscribe so the retest finds you, and leave today's number in the comments where you cannot hide from it. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
